stem: You run `git rebase main` on a feature branch whose two commits were made before `main` moved forward. What happens to the commit IDs of those two feature commits?

options.text: The IDs stay the same and only the branch pointer moves
options.why: That describes a fast-forward, not a rebase that replays commits.

options.text: Each replayed commit gets a new ID
options.why: Rebase creates new commits with new parents, so every replayed commit has a new hash.

options.text: Both keep their IDs, because their file changes are unchanged
options.why: A commit ID hashes the parent too, so a new parent always means a new ID.

options.text: Only the newest commit gets a new ID; the older one is reused
options.why: Every replayed commit has a new parent chain, so none of them can be reused.

explanation: A commit ID is a hash of the tree, the parent IDs, the author, the committer and the message. Rebase replays each commit on a new base, so each one gets a new parent and therefore a new ID. The old commits still exist until garbage collection, which is why `ORIG_HEAD` and the reflog can recover them.

stem: What is the "golden rule" of rebasing?

options.text: Never rebase commits that others may have based work on
options.why: Rewriting shared commits forces every collaborator to reconcile duplicate history.

options.text: Always rebase before every push, even on shared branches
options.why: Rebasing shared branches is exactly what the rule warns against.

options.text: Only rebase branches that contain merge commits
options.why: Merge commits are irrelevant to the rule; sharing is what matters.

options.text: Rebase only onto tags, never onto branches
options.why: You normally rebase onto a branch such as main; tags have nothing to do with it.

explanation: Rebase abandons existing commits and creates new ones. If someone has already pulled the old commits and built on them, their history now diverges from yours and they must untangle duplicate commits. Rebase local or private work freely; integrate shared branches with merges.
reference: Pro Git: The Perils of Rebasing

stem: `git commit --amend` edits the last commit in place, so its commit ID stays the same.

options.text: True
options.why: Amending writes a brand-new commit object; the old one is replaced, not edited.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: amending creates a new commit with a new ID, and the branch moves to it.

explanation: Git objects are immutable. `--amend` builds a new commit from the current index (and message) with the same parent as the old one, then moves the branch to it. The old commit stays in the reflog until it is garbage-collected. If the old commit was already pushed, the next normal push is rejected.

stem: In an interactive rebase todo list, which command merges a commit into the one above it and discards the commit's own message?

options.text: `fixup`
options.why: fixup melds the change into the previous commit and drops this commit's message.

options.text: `squash`
options.why: squash also melds the commit, but it keeps both messages for you to edit.

options.text: `drop`
options.why: drop removes the commit and its change entirely.

options.text: `reword`
options.why: reword keeps the commit separate and only lets you edit its message.

explanation: `squash` and `fixup` both fold a commit into the previous one. `squash` opens the editor with both messages combined; `fixup` keeps only the earlier commit's message. `fixup -C` is a variant that keeps the fixup commit's message instead.

stem: What does `git cherry-pick <sha>` do?

options.text: Applies that commit's change as a new commit on the current branch
options.why: It replays the diff the commit introduced and commits it with a new ID.

options.text: Merges the whole branch that contains the commit into the current one
options.why: Only that one commit's change is applied, not the branch history.

options.text: Moves the commit onto the current branch and deletes it at the source
options.why: The original commit stays where it is; cherry-pick copies its change.

options.text: Checks out the commit in a detached HEAD so you can inspect it
options.why: That is `git switch --detach <sha>`, not cherry-pick.

explanation: Cherry-pick computes the change a commit introduced relative to its parent and applies it on top of HEAD as a new commit, reusing the original message and author. The new commit has a different ID because it has a different parent.

stem: Match each interactive-rebase todo command with what it does.

options.text: Use the commit but edit its message
Stop after applying the commit so you can amend it
Use the commit unchanged
Remove the commit and its change

explanation: `pick` replays the commit as is. `reword` replays it and opens the editor for the message. `edit` replays it and pauses, so you can amend it, split it, or add commits before running `git rebase --continue`. `drop` removes it from the rewritten history.

stem: A `git rebase main` stops with a conflict in `app.js`. You fix the file. What do you run next?

options.text: `git rebase --skip`, to keep your resolved file
options.why: skip drops the whole commit being replayed, including your fix.

options.text: `git merge --continue`, because conflicts are a merge step
options.why: You are in a rebase, so the rebase must be continued, not a merge.

options.text: `git commit --amend`, then `git push`
options.why: The rebase is still in progress; amending and pushing leaves it half-finished.

options.text: `git add app.js`, then `git rebase --continue`
options.why: Staging marks the conflict resolved; --continue commits it and replays the rest.

explanation: During a rebase, Git stops at each commit that conflicts. Resolve the file, stage it with `git add`, then run `git rebase --continue`, which records the commit and moves on. `--skip` drops the current commit; `--abort` restores the branch to where it was before the rebase.

stem: You rewrote a branch you had already pushed. Complete the safer force-push option, which refuses to overwrite remote commits you haven't seen: `git push --force-____-lease`. Type the missing word.
explanation: `--force-with-lease` only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where your remote-tracking ref says it does. Plain `--force` overwrites unconditionally. The lease is weaker than it looks if a background fetch updated your tracking ref, which is why `--force-if-includes` exists.

stem:
Starting from this history, you run the commands below. What does `git log --format=%s` print?

```text
main:  A - B
        \
feat:    F1 - F2
```

```bash
git switch feat
git rebase main
```

options.why: F1 and F2 are replayed on top of B, so the history becomes linear.
Rebase never interleaves upstream commits between your commits.
Your commits go on top of the new base, not underneath it.

options.text: `F2, F1, A` (B is not included)
options.why: feat now sits on top of main, so B is part of its history.

explanation: Rebase finds the commits on `feat` that aren't on `main` (F1, F2), moves to the tip of `main`, commit B, and replays them in order. The result is A - B - F1' - F2', newest first in `git log`.

stem: On branch `main`, which commits does `git cherry-pick X1..X3` apply, given the source branch has X1, X2 and X3 in that order?

options.text: Only X3
options.why: A range applies every commit in it, not only the last one.

options.text: X1 and X2
options.why: X3 is the end of the range and is included.

options.text: X2 and X3
options.why: A..B means "reachable from B but not from A", so X1 is left out.

options.text: X1, X2 and X3
options.why: The range A..B excludes A itself; use X1^..X3 to include it.

explanation: Cherry-pick ranges use the same rule as `git log A..B`: commits reachable from B but not from A. So `X1..X3` applies X2 and X3. To include the first commit, write `X1^..X3`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You pushed `main`, then ran `git commit --amend` to fix the message. What does `git status -sb` show on its first line, and why?

options.text: `## main...origin/main [ahead 1, behind 1]`
options.why: Your new commit isn't on the remote, and the old one is no longer in your branch.

options.text: `## main...origin/main [behind 1]`, since the amend removed a commit
options.why: The amended commit is new, so you are also ahead by one.

options.text: `## main...origin/main`, because the content is unchanged
options.why: Git compares commits, not content; the IDs now differ.

options.text: `## main...origin/main [ahead 1]`, since the amend added a commit
options.why: Amending replaces the last commit rather than adding one.

explanation: The amended commit replaced the pushed one, so the branches have diverged: one commit only you have, and one only the remote has. A normal `git push` is rejected as non-fast-forward; you need a force push (preferably with a lease), which is why amending pushed commits is discouraged.

stem: You ran `git commit --fixup a1b2c3` (the commit "Add login") and later `git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `--fixup` changes "Add login" immediately, so its ID changes at commit time
options.why: Nothing is rewritten until you run the rebase.

options.text: Autosquash moves it right after "Add login" and marks it `fixup`
options.why: The todo list is reordered automatically before the editor opens.

options.text: You must edit the todo list by hand to move the fixup line
options.why: That manual step is exactly what --autosquash automates.

options.text: The fixup commit's subject is `fixup! Add login`
options.why: --fixup builds the subject from the target commit so autosquash can find it.

options.text: The combined commit keeps both messages, like `squash`
options.why: A fixup discards its own message; only "Add login" survives.

explanation: `git commit --fixup <commit>` records a normal commit whose subject is `fixup! <subject of target>`. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash` (or `rebase.autoSquash=true`) moves that commit directly after its target and changes `pick` to `fixup`, folding the change in without keeping the extra message. Verified: the result was "Add logout, Add login, A" with the fixed content.

stem: `git cherry-pick -x <sha>` appends a line like "(cherry picked from commit <sha>)" to the new commit's message.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: -x records where the change came from, which helps when backporting fixes.

options.text: False
options.why: It does add the line; that is the whole purpose of -x.

explanation: The `-x` option appends "(cherry picked from commit …)" to the message. It is useful for cherry-picks from public branches, such as backports to release branches, because reviewers can trace the original commit. Avoid it for private branches whose commits will be rewritten.

stem: Your local `main` and `origin/main` have diverged, and `pull.rebase` and `pull.ff` aren't set. Plain `git pull` fails. Which two commands complete the pull? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git pull --rebase`
options.why: It replays your local commit on top of the fetched ones.

options.text: `git pull --no-rebase`
options.why: It merges the fetched commits, creating a merge commit.

options.text: `git pull --ff-only`
options.why: The branches have diverged, so a fast-forward is impossible and it fails.

options.text: `git pull --squash`
options.why: A squash merge stages changes without recording a merge; it doesn't reconcile the histories.

options.text: `git pull --force`
options.why: --force only affects ref updates during fetch; it doesn't choose a reconcile method.

explanation: Since Git 2.33, a pull with divergent branches and no configured strategy stops with "fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches." Choose explicitly: `--rebase` (or `pull.rebase true`) for linear history, `--no-rebase` (or `pull.rebase false`) to merge, or `--ff-only`, which only succeeds when no local commits exist. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Put these steps in order to combine your last three local commits into one and update the already-pushed branch.

options.text: Save and close the todo list
Run `git push --force-with-lease`
Change the second and third `pick` lines to `squash`
Run `git rebase -i HEAD~3`
Edit the combined commit message and save

explanation: Interactive rebase opens the todo list (oldest commit first). Mark the later commits `squash` (or `fixup`), save, and Git replays them into one commit and asks for the combined message. Because the branch was already pushed, its history changed, so the update needs a force push; a lease makes it refuse if someone else pushed in the meantime.

stem: Your branch has 2 commits ahead of `main`. How many times does `git rebase --exec "npm test" main` run `npm test`? Type a number.
explanation: `--exec` adds an `exec` line after every replayed commit in the todo list, so the command runs once per commit: twice here. If the command fails, the rebase stops so you can fix that commit. This is a common way to make sure every commit in a series builds. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem:
An interactive rebase has this todo list, and you accept the proposed message without editing it. What is the resulting commit's message?

```text
pick   1a1 B1
squash 2b2 B2
fixup  3c3 B3
```

options.text: Only `B3`, the newest message
options.why: Plain fixup never keeps its own message; that would need `fixup -C`.

options.text: `B1`, then a blank line, then `B2`
options.why: squash keeps its message; fixup throws its message away.

options.text: Only `B1`
options.why: The squash line contributes its message to the combined text.

options.text: `B1`, `B2` and `B3`, separated by blank lines
options.why: The fixup commit's message is discarded.

explanation: All three commits are melded into one. `squash` adds its message to the message being built; `fixup` contributes only its change. Accepting the editor without changes keeps the non-comment lines, so the message is "B1", a blank line, and "B2". Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You start `git rebase main` with an unstaged edit to a tracked file. What happens?

options.text: The edit is silently discarded so the rebase can run
options.why: Git protects uncommitted work rather than throwing it away.

options.text: It refuses: "cannot rebase: You have unstaged changes"
options.why: Rebase needs a clean worktree unless you ask it to stash for you.

options.text: The edit is committed into the first replayed commit
options.why: Rebase never commits unstaged work on its own.

options.text: It proceeds and keeps the edit only if no file conflicts
options.why: It doesn't try; it stops before starting.

explanation: Rebase requires a clean working tree. Either commit or stash first, or use `git rebase --autostash` (or `rebase.autoStash=true`), which creates a temporary stash, runs the rebase and reapplies the stash at the end. Verified: the edit was preserved after `--autostash`.

stem: `git rebase -i HEAD~3` opens the todo list. Is the newest of the three commits on the first line or the last line? Type `first` or `last`.
explanation: The todo list is in the order the commits will be replayed: oldest at the top, newest at the bottom. That is the reverse of `git log`, a common source of mistakes when reordering or squashing.

stem: Your feature branch has five commits and `main` has moved on. Which two statements correctly compare `git rebase main` with `git merge main` on the feature branch? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rebase resolves all conflicts once, for the whole branch
options.why: Rebase may stop at each commit that conflicts.

options.text: Rebase records when the integration happened in a merge commit
options.why: That is what merge does; rebase records no integration point.

options.text: Rebase rewrites the feature commits, so a pushed branch needs a force push
options.why: New IDs mean the remote branch no longer matches.

options.text: Rebase gives a linear history with no merge commit
options.why: Your commits are replayed on top of main.

options.text: Rebase keeps the original commit IDs, so it is safe on shared branches
options.why: Replayed commits always get new IDs.

explanation: Merge keeps history exactly as it happened and adds a merge commit, resolving conflicts once. Rebase produces a cleaner linear history but rewrites your commits, may make you resolve conflicts commit by commit, and requires force-pushing if the branch was already pushed.

stem: Branch `feat` changed line 1 of `f` to "feature"; `main` changed it to "main". During `git rebase main` on `feat`, the conflict stops the rebase. What does `git checkout --ours f` put in the file?

options.text: The original "base" line from the merge base
options.why: --ours picks one side; neither side is the base.

options.text: Nothing; `--ours` isn't allowed during a rebase
options.why: It is allowed; the meaning of the sides is what changes.

options.text: "main"
options.why: During a rebase, "ours" is the branch you are replaying onto.

options.text: "feature"
options.why: That is "theirs" during a rebase: the commit being replayed.

explanation: Rebase works by checking out the upstream and replaying your commits on top. So HEAD (ours) is the upstream side plus anything already replayed, and "theirs" is your commit being applied. This is the reverse of a merge on your branch, where ours is your branch. Verified: `--ours` gave "main", `--theirs` gave "feature".

stem: You export two commits with `git format-patch -2` and apply them in another repository. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It writes one `.patch` file per commit, such as `0001-Add-two.patch`
options.why: Each commit becomes a numbered mbox-format patch.

options.text: `git am` only works with patches fetched from a configured remote
options.why: am reads local mbox files; no remote is involved.

options.text: `git apply` on a patch creates a commit with the original message
options.why: apply only changes the working tree; it never commits.

options.text: `git am` on those files creates commits that keep the author and message
options.why: am reads the email headers and recreates the commits.

options.text: `format-patch -2` writes one combined patch for both commits
options.why: Each commit gets its own file.

explanation: `git format-patch` writes one email-style file per commit, including author, date and message. `git am` applies them and recreates the commits; `git apply` just patches the working tree (and optionally the index) without committing. Verified: am produced "Add two" and "Add three"; apply left `a` modified with no new commit.

stem:
History is shown below. You run `git rebase --onto main server client`. What is `client`'s history afterwards, newest first?

```text
main:    A - B - M1
              \
server:        S1 - S2
                 \
client:           C1 - C2
```

options.text: C2, C1, S1, M1, B, A
options.why: S1 is reachable from server, so it isn't replayed.

options.text: C2, C1, M1, B, A
options.why: Only commits in server..client (C1, C2) move, onto main.

options.text: C2, C1, S1, B, A (unchanged)
options.why: --onto main moves the replayed commits onto main's tip.
The server commits are excluded by the second argument.

explanation: `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>` replays the commits in `upstream..branch` onto `newbase`. Here that is `server..client` = C1 and C2, transplanted onto main. `server` is untouched and you end up on `client`. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Your feature branch contains a merge commit (you merged a helper branch into it). You run `git rebase main` without extra options. What happens to that merge?

options.text: It is replayed as an empty commit with the merge message
options.why: Merge commits are skipped, not turned into empty commits.

options.text: It disappears: its changes are replayed as linear commits
options.why: By default rebase drops merge commits and replays the non-merge commits.

options.text: The rebase refuses to start because merge commits can't be replayed
options.why: It doesn't refuse; it linearises the history.

options.text: It is kept as a merge commit, recreated on top of the new base
options.why: That needs --rebase-merges; the default flattens.

explanation: By default, rebase only replays non-merge commits, so a branch containing merges becomes linear. `--rebase-merges` recreates the merge topology instead. Verified: the default left 0 merge commits; `--rebase-merges` kept 1.

stem: Commit "fix X" on `feat` was cherry-picked to `main` as "fix X cherry" with the identical change. You then run `git rebase main` on `feat`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Both "fix X" and "fix X cherry" end up in the new history
options.why: The duplicate is dropped from the replayed commits.

options.text: Rebase skips "fix X" because main already contains the same patch
options.why: Rebase compares patch IDs and drops changes already upstream.

options.text: Rebase stops with a conflict on "fix X"
options.why: An identical change applies cleanly, and it is skipped anyway.

options.text: The skip works even though the two messages differ
options.why: Patch IDs ignore the message and depend only on the diff.

options.text: Rebase only skips commits whose SHA already exists on main
options.why: The cherry-pick has a different SHA; matching uses the patch content.

explanation: Before replaying, rebase excludes commits whose patch ID (a hash of the diff) matches a commit already in upstream. That avoids duplicate changes after a cherry-pick or an applied patch. Verified: after the rebase the log was "Y, fix X cherry, A".

stem: You try `git cherry-pick <merge-sha>` to bring a merge commit onto a release branch, and Git refuses. What does `-m 1` tell it?

options.text: Apply only the first commit that was made on the merged branch
options.why: -m selects a parent, not a commit from the merged branch.

options.text: Record the cherry-picked merge with a one-line commit message
options.why: -m here is "mainline", not a message flag.

options.text: Diff against parent 1 (the mainline) and apply the result
options.why: A merge has two parents; -m picks which one to diff against.

options.text: Skip the merge itself and cherry-pick its first parent commit instead
options.why: The merge's own change is applied relative to the chosen parent.

explanation: A merge commit has no single diff, so cherry-pick stops with "is a merge but no -m option was given". `-m 1` treats the first parent (usually the branch that was merged into) as the mainline and applies the difference the merge introduced relative to it, which is the side branch's work. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: `part2` is built on top of `part1`, a stacked branch. `main` moved on. On `part2` you run `git rebase main` with no other options. Where is `part1` afterwards?

options.text: It is moved onto main together with part2
options.why: Only the branch being rebased moves unless you ask for --update-refs.

options.text: It is deleted because its commit was rewritten
options.why: Rebase never deletes other branches.

options.text: It still points at its old commit on the old base
options.why: part1's ref isn't touched, so the stack is now split.

options.text: It becomes a detached HEAD
options.why: A branch ref can't become a detached HEAD; it just stays where it was.

explanation: Rebase rewrites the commits of the branch you are on, including P1 in this case, but leaves other refs alone. `part1` keeps pointing at the old P1, so the stack splits. `git rebase --update-refs` (or `rebase.updateRefs=true`) also moves branch refs that point at rewritten commits. Verified: without it part1 was "P1, A"; with it, "P1, M, A".

stem: A large binary was committed early in a repository's history and later deleted. Which two statements are true about removing it from the history? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git rm` plus a new commit removes it from earlier commits too
options.why: Earlier commits still contain the file; only new snapshots lose it.

options.text: `git gc` removes it immediately, even if old refs still point at it
options.why: Objects reachable from any ref or reflog are kept.

options.text: After force-pushing, collaborators must re-clone or rebase their work
options.why: Their branches are still built on the old history.

options.text: Every commit from the first one containing it gets a new ID
options.why: Rewriting an old commit changes it and everything that descends from it.

options.text: git filter-repo keeps all the original commit IDs
options.why: Any history rewrite changes the IDs of rewritten commits.

explanation: Commits are immutable snapshots, so a file is removed from history only by rewriting every commit that contains it with a tool such as git filter-repo or BFG. That changes those commits' IDs and all their descendants, needs a force push, and every collaborator must re-clone or rebase. Old copies stay reachable through other refs, reflogs and clones until those are cleaned too.
reference: git-filter-repo documentation; Pro Git: Rewriting History

stem: After you rewrite history to remove a leaked secret and force-push, the secret is gone from every clone and fork.

options.text: True
options.why: Clones, forks, caches and CI logs keep their copies; only your remote ref changed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: existing copies keep the old commits, so the secret must still be rotated.

explanation: Force-pushing only changes the refs on the remote you pushed to. Every clone, every fork, pull request refs on the hosting platform, CI caches and anyone who fetched still have the old objects. Treat any pushed secret as compromised: revoke and rotate it first, then clean history to stop further spread.
reference: GitHub docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository

stem: During `git rebase main`, the commit "conflicting" (which edits `f`) conflicts. You run `git rebase --skip`. What happens?

options.text: Your resolved version of `f` is kept and committed automatically
options.why: skip discards that commit's change entirely.

options.text: The conflicting commit is dropped and the rest are replayed
options.why: skip throws away the commit currently being applied.

options.text: Git keeps the conflict markers in the file and carries on replaying
options.why: skip resets to the last good state before moving on.

options.text: The whole rebase is cancelled and the branch is restored
options.why: That is --abort.

explanation: `git rebase --skip` drops the commit being replayed and continues with the next one, so that commit's change is lost from the rewritten branch. Verified: after skipping, the log was "other, main change, base" and `f` held main's version. Use it only when the commit is genuinely redundant.

stem: Match each cherry-pick command with what it does.

options.text: Applies C and records its source commit in the message
Applies C's change without committing it
Applies A through B, including A
Applies the commits after A up to and including B

explanation: Ranges follow `git log` rules, so `A..B` excludes A and `A^..B` includes it. `-x` appends "(cherry picked from commit …)". `-n` (`--no-commit`) stages the change without committing, which lets you combine several picks into one commit.

stem: Carol rebases Dave's branch onto `main` on her machine. What does `git log --format="%an / %cn"` show for Dave's replayed commits?

options.text: `Dave / Dave`
options.why: The committer is whoever created the new commit object: Carol.

options.text: `Carol / Dave`
options.why: This swaps the two roles.

options.text: `Dave / Carol`
options.why: Author is preserved; committer becomes the person who ran the rebase.

options.text: `Carol / Carol`
options.why: Rebase keeps the original author.

explanation: Git tracks an author (who wrote the change) and a committer (who created this commit object). Rebase, cherry-pick and amend keep the author but set the committer, and committer date, to whoever ran the command. Verified with Git 2.55.
reference: Pro Git: Viewing the Commit History (author vs committer)

stem: Your team "Squash and merge"s a PR on GitHub. You keep committing on the same branch and open a second PR. Why does the new PR also list the commits from the first one?

options.text: main has one squashed commit, not your individual commits
options.why: Those commits aren't reachable from main, so the branch still appears to contain them.

options.text: Squash merging resets the source branch to the PR's base commit
options.why: Nothing is reset; the branch is simply unchanged.

options.text: The second PR was opened against the wrong base
options.why: Even with the right base, those commits aren't in main.

options.text: GitHub caches the commit list of a branch from its earlier PR
options.why: PR commit lists are computed from the branches each time.

explanation: A squash merge creates one new commit on main containing the combined change, so your original commits never become part of main's history. Further work on the same branch still sits on top of them. Start a new branch from the updated main, or `git rebase --onto origin/main <last-old-commit>` to move only the new commits.
reference: GitHub docs: About pull request merges

stem: Your branch has commits A, B, C (oldest first). In the todo from `git rebase -i HEAD~2` you delete the line for B, leaving no `drop` keyword. With default settings, what happens?

options.text: B is replayed anyway, at the end of the list
options.why: The todo list is authoritative; omitted commits aren't replayed.

options.text: The rebase pauses at B so you can decide
options.why: Only `edit` or a conflict pauses the rebase.

options.text: Git aborts because a commit line is missing
options.why: It only checks for missing lines if `rebase.missingCommitsCheck` is set.

options.text: B is removed from the rewritten history
options.why: A deleted line means the commit isn't replayed: the same as drop.

explanation: Removing a line has the same effect as `drop`. `rebase.missingCommitsCheck` defaults to `ignore`; set it to `warn` or `error` to guard against accidental deletions. Verified: the log became "C, A".

stem: Alice amended a pushed commit. Meanwhile Bob pushed a commit to `main`. Alice's IDE then ran a background `git fetch`. Alice runs `git push --force-with-lease origin main`. What happens?

options.text: It succeeds and keeps Bob's commit on top
options.why: A force push replaces the branch; nothing is merged.

options.text: It is rejected as "stale info" because Bob's commit is new
options.why: The fetch already updated origin/main, so the lease no longer sees it as new.

options.text: It is rejected because amended commits can't be force-pushed
options.why: Amended commits can be force-pushed; that is the usual workflow.

options.text: It succeeds and Bob's commit disappears from the remote
options.why: The lease checks against origin/main, which the fetch moved to Bob's commit.

explanation: Without an explicit expected value, `--force-with-lease` compares the remote branch with your remote-tracking ref. A background fetch updates that ref, so the lease passes even though Alice never looked at Bob's commit, and the push overwrites it. Verified with Git 2.55: before the fetch the push was rejected; after it, the remote held only Alice's rewritten commit.

stem: In the scenario where a background fetch defeated `--force-with-lease`, which addition makes Git reject Alice's push?

options.text: `--atomic`
options.why: Atomic makes multi-ref pushes all-or-nothing; it doesn't check what you've seen.

options.text: `--force-if-includes`
options.why: It also requires the remote tip to be in Alice's local reflog, i.e. integrated by her.

options.text: `--no-verify`
options.why: That skips the pre-push hook; it adds no safety.

options.text: `--prune`
options.why: Prune deletes remote branches with no local counterpart.

explanation: `--force-if-includes` (Git 2.30+) works with `--force-with-lease`. It checks that the remote tip being overwritten is reachable from an entry in your local branch's reflog, meaning you actually integrated it, not just fetched it. Verified: with both options the push was rejected. An explicit lease, `--force-with-lease=main:<expected-sha>`, also works.

stem: An API key was committed and pushed three weeks ago. Which three actions belong in the response? (Choose three.)

options.text: `git revert` the commit, which removes the key from history
options.why: Revert adds a new commit; the old one still contains the key.

options.text: Ask collaborators to re-clone or rebase onto the cleaned history
options.why: Old clones would reintroduce the commits if pushed back.

options.text: Revoke and rotate the key immediately
options.why: The key must be assumed compromised the moment it was pushed.

options.text: Delete the file in a new commit and keep the key
options.why: The key stays in history and anyone who saw it can use it.

options.text: Make the repository private, which makes the leaked key safe again
options.why: Anyone who already copied it still has it.

options.text: Rewrite history with git filter-repo or BFG and force-push
options.why: This stops the key spreading further through new clones.

explanation: Rotate first: once pushed, the secret may already be scraped, cloned or cached. Then purge it from history with git filter-repo or BFG, force-push every affected branch and tag, ask the hosting provider to purge cached views and PR refs if needed, and make collaborators re-clone so the old commits aren't pushed back.
reference: GitHub docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository

stem: A teammate rewrote `origin/feature` (rebased it onto main). Your branch `mine` was built on the old `feature` tip `abc123`. After `git fetch`, which command moves only your own commits onto the new `origin/feature`?

options.text: `git merge origin/feature` on `mine`
options.why: This drags in both old and new versions of the rewritten commits.

options.text: `git rebase origin/feature mine`
options.why: It may try to replay the teammate's old pre-rewrite commits too.

options.text: `git rebase --onto origin/feature abc123 mine`
options.why: Only commits in abc123..mine are replayed onto the new feature tip.

options.text: `git reset --hard origin/feature` on `mine`
options.why: This throws your own commits away.

explanation: After an upstream rewrite, your branch still contains the old upstream commits. `git rebase --onto <new-upstream> <old-upstream-tip> <branch>` replays only your commits. Plain `git rebase origin/feature` (or `git pull --rebase`) may manage it through the fork-point reflog and patch-ID detection, but that fails when the reflog no longer has the old tip or the patches changed.
reference: git-rebase documentation: Recovering from upstream rebase

stem: Commit "Fix" on `feat` was cherry-picked to `main`. Later `feat` (still containing the original "Fix") is merged into `main`. What happens?

options.text: Git detects the duplicate change and drops one of the two commits
options.why: Only rebase does patch-ID skipping; merge never does.

options.text: The merge refuses until the cherry-pick is reverted
options.why: There is no such check.

options.text: The merge conflicts on the files "Fix" touched
options.why: Both sides made the identical change, so the three-way merge is clean.

options.text: It merges cleanly and history contains two "Fix" commits
options.why: Same change, different IDs: Git doesn't deduplicate commits on merge.

explanation: A three-way merge compares trees, not commits. Since both sides made the same change, there is no conflict, but both commits remain in history with different IDs. Verified: `git log --grep=Fix` listed two commits. If the code around the change diverged later, such duplicates can still conflict.

stem: Your local `main` has commit U2; `origin/main` has a new commit U1 that you don't have. You run `git pull --rebase`. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: U2 is replayed on top of U1 and gets a new ID
options.why: Your local commit is rebased onto the fetched tip.

options.text: U1 is replayed on top of U2
options.why: Remote commits are never rewritten by your pull.

options.text: U1's ID changes because it is rebased too
options.why: Only your unpublished local commits are rewritten.

options.text: The log reads U2, U1, base, newest first
options.why: Remote work stays underneath, your commit on top.

options.text: No merge commit is created
options.why: Pull with rebase linearises instead of merging.

explanation: `git pull --rebase` fetches, then rebases your local commits onto the updated upstream. Remote commits keep their IDs; yours are replayed on top with new IDs, and no merge commit is created. Verified: the log was "U2, U1, base".

stem:
Your todo list is shown below. After the rebase, what is the message of the single resulting commit?

```text
pick      1a1 old message
fixup -C  2b2 better message
```

options.text: `better message`
options.why: `fixup -C` uses the fixup commit's message instead of the earlier one.

options.text: `old message`
options.why: Plain fixup would keep it; `-C` changes that.

options.text: The editor opens because the messages conflict
options.why: `-C` takes the message without opening the editor; `-c` would open it.

options.text: Both messages, separated by a blank line
options.why: That is what squash produces.

explanation: `fixup -C <commit>` melds the change like `fixup` but replaces the message with this commit's message. `fixup -c` does the same and opens the editor. It is handy with `git commit --fixup=reword:<commit>`, which creates an "amend!" commit for autosquash. Verified: the result was "better message".

stem: You change the first `pick` in an interactive todo list to `squash` and save. What happens?

options.text: The squash is ignored and the commit is picked
options.why: Git reports the problem instead of silently changing your instruction.

options.text: The commit is dropped
options.why: Nothing is dropped; the rebase stops with an error.

options.text: Git errors: "cannot 'squash' without a previous commit"
options.why: squash needs a previous todo commit to meld into.

options.text: The commit is squashed into the commit before the rebase range
options.why: The base commit isn't part of the todo list, so there is nothing above it to squash into.

explanation: Squash and fixup combine a commit with the one before it in the todo list, so the first line can't be one. Git stops with "cannot 'squash' without a previous commit" and suggests `git rebase --edit-todo`. To squash into an older commit, start the rebase earlier (for example `HEAD~4`). Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: During `git rebase -i`, you marked commit B as `edit` so you can split it in two. The rebase stopped after applying B. What sequence splits it?

options.text: `git reset HEAD^`, stage and commit each part, then `git rebase --continue`
options.why: Undo B but keep its changes, then recommit them as two commits.

options.text: `git rebase --skip`, then commit the two parts by hand
options.why: skip drops B's change entirely before you can split it.

options.text: `git commit --amend` twice, then `git rebase --continue`
options.why: Amending replaces B each time; you still end up with one commit.

options.text: `git cherry-pick -n B` twice, then `git rebase --continue`
options.why: That reapplies B's whole change twice rather than splitting it.

explanation: `edit` stops with B already committed. `git reset HEAD^` (a mixed reset) moves the branch back to B's parent but keeps B's changes in the working tree. Stage and commit the first part, then the second, and run `git rebase --continue` to replay the remaining commits on top.

stem: A colleague emails you a patch made with `git format-patch`. You want it recorded as a commit with their name and message, falling back to a 3-way merge if the context changed. Which command?

options.text: `git apply --3way 0001-fix.patch`
options.why: apply never creates a commit, so the authorship and message are lost.

options.text: `git cherry-pick 0001-fix.patch`
options.why: cherry-pick takes commits, not patch files.

options.text: `git am -3 0001-fix.patch`
options.why: am creates the commit from the email headers; -3 enables the 3-way fallback.

options.text: `git merge 0001-fix.patch`
options.why: merge takes branches or commits, not patch files.

explanation: `git am` turns mbox patches into commits, preserving the author, date and message. `-3` (`--3way`) lets it fall back to a three-way merge using the blob IDs recorded in the patch when the surrounding lines have changed. `git apply` only patches files and leaves committing to you.

stem: Put these internal steps of `git rebase main` (run on `feat`) in the order Git performs them.

options.text: Point feat at the last replayed commit and record ORIG_HEAD
Find the merge base of feat and main
Replay each listed commit in order
Check out main's tip as a detached HEAD
List the commits on feat not in main, skipping patches already upstream

explanation: Rebase first works out which commits are unique to your branch (from the merge base, excluding patch-identical ones), detaches HEAD at the new base, applies each commit in turn, and finally moves the branch ref to the result. The old tip is saved in ORIG_HEAD and the reflog. Until the last step, `git rebase --abort` can restore the original branch.
